title: Unsecured Credentials: Group Policy Preferences
summary: Group Policy Preferences allow administrators to push settings, including local account passwords, to domain computers. When such a password is configured, Windows stores it in XML files under the SYSVOL share of a domain controller, protected only by an AES key that Microsoft published in its own documentation years ago. Because SYSVOL is readable by every authenticated domain user, any account on the domain can copy the XML, extract the cpassword attribute and recover the plaintext with the public key. Defenders rarely see malware at all here: the artefacts are ordinary file reads of SYSVOL policy files, followed by authentication with the recovered account. Detection therefore leans on file access auditing of the domain controller share and on process creation events for scripting or decryption tooling, and on the sudden use of a service account that had no interactive activity before.

beginner.definition: Group Policy Preferences are a Windows feature that lets administrators set options on many computers at once, for example a shared local account password. When that password is saved, Windows keeps it in a file on the domain controller with only simple encryption. Attackers who can read that file can work out the real password.
beginner.whyItMatters: The encrypted password sits in a share that every normal domain user can read. The key that unlocks it was published by Microsoft, so the protection is almost none. One old policy file can therefore hand an attacker a working account. That account often works on many computers across the company.
howItWorks: An administrator creates a policy that sets a local account password on many computers.
Windows saves that password inside an XML policy file in the SYSVOL share.
The password is scrambled with a key that Microsoft published for everyone to see.
Every signed-in domain user can copy that policy file because SYSVOL is shared to them.
The attacker then decrypts that value and learns the real plaintext password.
The attacker signs in with that account and moves to other computers.
beginner.example: Imagine a caretaker who hides the master key to a block of flats inside a locked box by the front door. The box has a simple lock, and the caretaker helpfully tapes the code to the door frame for anyone who asks. Every resident walks past that box each day. One resident copies the code, opens the box, and now holds the key to every flat in the building. Group Policy Preferences work the same way: the password is locked, but the unlocking key is public.
takeaways: Passwords inside old Group Policy Preference files are effectively public, so find and delete them.
File permissions do not hide a secret when the encryption key is public.
Watch for unusual reads of SYSVOL files and for accounts that suddenly log in elsewhere.

objectives: Explain why Group Policy Preferences can expose local account passwords.
Describe where the password value is stored and who can read it.
Identify which log sources show unexpected reads of SYSVOL policy files.
Recognise signs that a recovered service account is being used for lateral movement.
Recommend how to find and remove password data from Group Policy Preference files.
